episode.title: Deadly Flooding in Nepal Highlights Asia’s Climate Vulnerability
episode.description:
Hundreds of hydropower workers remain missing in Nepal after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic flooding. The disaster laid bare the rising climate risks across Asia and the danger of building in an increasingly volatile environment.

On today’s Big Take Asia podcast, guest host Rebecca Choong Wilkins sits down with Bloomberg’s Clara Ferreira Marques and Bloomberg Opinion’s David Fickling to talk about the human and economic toll of the disaster, why the catastrophe is a warning for the rest of the world and how Nepal’s big bet on clean energy may now be at risk.

We have a special Bloomberg subscription offer for podcast listeners at Bloomberg.com/podcastoffer.

Hosted by Rebecca Choong Wilkins; Produced by Yang Yang; Reported by Clara Ferreira Marques, David Fickling; Edited by Paddy Hirsch, Crispina Robert and Tracey Samuelson.

Fact-checking by Naomi Ng; Engineering by Alex Sugiura

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: Countries affected by the kind of flooding that has hit northern Nepal are investing in a variety of measures to offset growing climate-related risks. Things like early warning systems to flag potential weaknesses, sponge cities to absorb and store rainwater and big infrastructure projects like dams, river dikes, and increasingly hydropower.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: A lot of the big hydro projects of the 20th century were built not so much for electricity, they were actually built for flood management and for flood control. And the hydroelectricity was the sort of co-benefit that paid for the flood control. That's the case with a lot of the big US dam projects. It's the case with the Three Gorges Dam in China.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: But not all hydropower projects are created equal. David says there are generally two types of hydropower dams, and one can offer significantly more protection against flooding than the other.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: One is called storage hydro and the other is called run-of-river hydro. Now, storage hydro is what we normally think about. It's a big dam that makes a reservoir. People are displaced from the reservoir that as, as that fills up, and then when you have this new reservoir like, you know, like Glen Canyon in the US or the Three Gorges in China. That's barely being built in places like Nepal. And what we have instead is something called run-of-river hydro, which is more like a water wheel. It doesn't create much of a reservoir. It doesn't disrupt the river flow very much. It's cheaper to build, but it doesn't provide the benefits of storing energy and doing flood management that you get from storage hydro. So Nepal is sort of building the cheaper version that doesn't provide flood protection.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: And yet hydropower is still an important pillar of the country's economic ambitions. It provides cheap electricity at home and is a source of export revenue abroad. But Nepal has struggled to fully capitalize on hydropower's potential.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: The biggest problem for Nepal is just that it's been a very poor country. It doesn't have a sophisticated electricity grid. About like 13% of electricity is lost every year just by, you know, general losses in the grid network. It's got very minimal integration with exports to India. And also these run-of-river dams, which are the ones that they're building, 90% of them are these run-of-river dams. They export electricity only when the water is running. They can't store it for later months. And that means they're often selling into the Indian market at the time when prices are lowest. So it's not very attractive.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: Disasters like the one playing out in northern Nepal right now complicate the picture. There are hundreds of hydro projects in the country, either in development or up and running. But about a dozen of them have been affected by these floods. That's already creating ripple effects through the hydropower industry as project companies call on their insurers to assess the damage.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: Obviously, an incident like this pushes up the cost of insurance. Insurers have been talking about this for decades at this point. The frequency of natural disasters is going up and that is increasing their costs. And that interacts with the fact, of course, that insurers, one side of their business is insured losses and the other side is the investment side of their business. And a lot of their investments have been struggling in recent years as well. So they're sort of squeezed on both ends. It's going to push up the cost of insurance quite considerably.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: David says that won't help an industry that's been pushed down the list for investment for more than two decades.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: The funding drought that hit hydro in the '90s has not really receded. Of all the money that was committed by the major development banks in 2022 to energy, hydro took just 2.8% of all of that money. And if you look since the Paris Agreement in 2015, the amount committed to hydro has been about $8.7 billion. Fossil fuels has received about $12 billion since the Paris Agreement. So fossil fuels since the Paris Agreement on climate change have actually received more funding from development banks than hydroelectricity. And that, I think, is, is clearly a failure. I think actually the fact that wind and solar and batteries are such a compelling energy generation, um, cocktail is in some ways a problem in itself because it provides a, a lot of, um, very easy bankable projects that sort of crowd out a lot of this hydro, which is quite hard. Wind, solar, and batteries provide pretty much guaranteed cash flows between 1 and 5 years of getting your financial sign-off, whereas hydro is more like 10 to 15 years.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: Despite all of those challenges, David doesn't see Nepal backing away from its bet on hydropower.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: I think every country should aspire towards development, and I think Nepal has great potential to be an export powerhouse of this sort. That's what we're seeing a lot of other, like, high-altitude countries doing. You know, Ethiopia has done very well from building the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, this one that was built. Tanzania just financed a dam which has just recently opened and is similarly successful. Laos is another example of this. So there are plenty of examples of countries that can do well from this.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: Hydropower presents an opportunity for Nepal, but the devastation from the recent flooding shows the risks in developing this industry. Nepal's new government has been in power less than 6 months. David says to be successful in developing hydro, it needs to make some changes to the way things are done, starting with proper oversight.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: At the moment, no one's really taking responsibility for the problem. So Nepal, they have a planning law in Nepal, but essentially in these high mountain valleys, these are a long way from the arm of the law. So are these buildings and roads being built in stable situations that aren't going to be affected by floods, or, or are they just being built wherever you can persuade local officials to let you build them. When institutions are actually capable of taking responsibility for this, they actually can mitigate some of the damage.

utterances.speaker: G
utterances.text: The Nepalese government estimates it will cost between $4 and $5 billion to rebuild after these floods. But David notes that this is the third such disaster to hit the region in as many years, and there's no way to tell when the next one will strike.

utterances.speaker: C
utterances.text: The more you look into it, the more you realize these are becoming annual events. And one thing that we see, we've been warning about for many years with climate change, is that you spend all your time just running on the spot, basically, because of course you're, you're dealing with the, with the previous disaster and the consequences from the previous disaster before the next disaster even hits.
